title: What would actually happen if you fell into quicksand?
description:
In films, quicksand swallows people whole. Physics says you'd stop at your waist: quicksand is about twice as dense as a person, so you float. Getting a foot out is the hard part, and the trick is to wiggle slowly, not to be pulled.

Sources:
- Liquefaction of quicksand under stress (Nature 437, 635, 2005; doi:10.1038/437635a) — Khaldoun, Eiser, Wegdam & Bonn, Nature; record in the University of Amsterdam repository (UvA-DARE): https://dare.uva.nl/id/8832cb7f-2014-4f2a-81a8-cef2beb39773
- Quicksand Science: Why It Traps, How to Escape (28 Sep 2005) — National Geographic (Nicholas Bakalar): https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/quicksand-science-why-it-traps-how-to-escape/
- Quicksand Myth Debunked: You Can Float Free — Live Science (Bjorn Carey): https://www.livescience.com/9373-quicksand-myth-debunked-float-free.html

Labels: the force of lifting a car is the researchers' estimate (for pulling one foot out at 1 cm a second; National Geographic says a medium-size car, Live Science a small one). The 'into two pieces' warning is study co-author Daniel Bonn's, quoted by National Geographic. The study is of salt-lake quicksand (Khaldoun, Eiser, Wegdam & Bonn, Nature 437, 635, 2005; doi:10.1038/437635a).
